1:
The opening is an exclamation rather than an argument. Clarke thinks whole volumes might be written on this verse and the two following without exhausting the subject, and observes that the apostle does not attempt to describe it — he calls on the world and the church to behold it and wonder at it. The interrogative adjective, he says, asks what great love both as to quantity and quality, since both ideas are in the original term. Gill reads the imperative in the same spirit: see, take notice, look by faith with wonder and astonishment, and observe what an instance of matchless love this is. Robertson supplies the grammar, noting that the word is a qualitative interrogative found only here in this writer and originally asking of what country or race a thing is, and that the perfect tense marks a completed endowment of the receiver; he quotes Brooke's judgment that the appeal is an effort to restore the waning enthusiasm of the readers and recall them to their first love. Barnes divides the love in kind and in degree — in kind the most tender and ennobling, in degree the most exalted — and compares a prince who should adopt a wandering, ragged orphan found in the streets, though even that would be a trifle beside what is meant here.

What the adoption rests on is Calvin's concern. It was no common honour the heavenly Father bestowed when he adopted us as children, and the word for bestowed means that it is from mere bounty and benevolence, so that the love is declared gratuitous; there is an impropriety in the language, he grants, but the apostle preferred speaking so rather than fail to express what had to be known. Against the sophists who say God foresees those worthy to be adopted, he answers that in that case the gift would not be gratuitous, and since adoption is the only cause of our salvation nothing is left to our worthiness — for why are we sons, except that God began to love us freely when we deserved hatred? He also prefers children to sons as the rendering, and notes that being called sons is not an idle expression, since it is God who with his own mouth declares us to be such. Henry says the same from the other side, that the Father adopts all the children of the Son, and finds it strange that the holy God is not ashamed to be called our Father — we who by nature are heirs of sin and by practice children of disobedience and ingratitude. Both Clarke and Robertson note the short parenthesis in the older manuscripts, and we are, which Clarke finds in a long list of versions and Robertson calls a reflection characteristic of this writer, omitted by the received text.

The last clause explains why so great a dignity is invisible. Clarke insists the verb means to acknowledge or approve rather than merely to know of, since the world knew well enough that such persons existed but did not approve of them — a use common in both Testaments. Henry draws out what the world misses: little does it think that these poor, humble, contemned ones are the favourites of heaven, and the disciples may bear it the better since their Lord was here unknown as well as they. Calvin treats the same fact as a trial to faith — it can hardly be inferred from our present state that God is a Father to us, since the devil so contrives all things as to obscure the benefit — and gives Isaac and Jacob as the example, both chosen by God, yet the one persecuted by Ishmael with taunts and the other by Esau with the sword. Wesley puts it in two strokes: they know not what to make of us, we are a mystery to them.
2:
The sentence sets a present possession against a hidden future. Gill distinguishes the stages of the adoption: it is secret in God's predestination and in the covenant of grace, open in regeneration, through faith in Christ and by the testimony of the Spirit. Barnes takes the present dignity to be worth dwelling on for its own sake, since even if nothing beyond were known it would be a grateful subject of reflection. On why the rest is withheld he offers two conjectures — that the coming state may be so unlike the present that no words would convey it, and that under a probation no more light may be furnished, lest we cease to be stimulated toward a world of light. Robertson makes something of the opening adverb, that dignity and duty are ours now, without waiting for the second coming; and he notes that the pronoun in the hidden clause is neuter, asking what rather than who — which, as Bengel says, suggests something unspeakable, contained in the likeness of God. Wesley adds that it does not yet appear even to ourselves.

Calvin thinks the point is that we act foolishly when we estimate what God has given us by the present state of things. As to the body we are dust and a shadow with death always before our eyes, so that we find always a hell within us; the more necessary it is that our thoughts be withdrawn from the present view, lest the miseries around us shake our faith in a felicity that lies hid. He reads the conditional particle as an adverb of time and takes the verb of Christ rather than of our estate, comparing Paul's word that our life is hid with Christ in God — for God defers the manifestation of our glory because Christ is not yet manifested in the power of his kingdom, and faith cannot stand otherwise than by looking to his coming. Clarke reads the clause the same way, of the second coming when Christ shall be manifested in his glorified human nature to judge the world; and he remarks that this writer had already seen that glory on the mount, where it must have been partly obscured, since the disciples were not then like him and could not have borne the sight. Robertson leaves the subject open, allowing either Christ or the manifestation just mentioned, and thinking it the better rendering here.

What the seeing does is the last question. Barnes takes it that there is an influence in beholding the Saviour which tends to transform us into his likeness, and understands the promised resemblance of the body raised, of character, of happiness and of glory. Wesley says the sight will be manifest and without a veil, and will transform us into the same likeness, the glory of God penetrating our inmost substance. Clarke expects to see him in the splendour of his majesty, in the glory of both natures. Calvin raises the objection the reason invites: if seeing Christ makes us like him, the wicked will have this in common with us, since they too shall see his glory. His answer is that the promise is of seeing him as a friend, which will not be their case — they will dread his presence and be filled with terror, his glory so dazzling their eyes that they will be stupefied, as Adam dreaded God's presence, and as God told Moses that no man shall see him and live. So far as the image of God is renewed in us we have eyes prepared to see him; and since that renewal is begun in so small a measure, we shall not behold him face to face until we are stripped of the corruption of the flesh. He enters one caution besides: the likeness is not equality, since there must be some difference between head and members.
3:
Gill says a true hope of the happiness that lies in likeness to Christ and in the vision of him is founded only on his person, blood, righteousness and sacrifice; it is not a hope every man has, being implanted in regeneration and bestowed as a free grace gift. Robertson observes that the preposition is one of resting upon rather than looking to, and reports the three ways it has been taken — upon Christ by Brooke, upon God by Smith, upon God in Christ by Westcott. Calvin draws the inference the verse is making: the desire for holiness should not grow cold because our happiness has not yet appeared, for the hope is sufficient, and though we have not Christ before our eyes, hoping in him cannot but stimulate us to follow purity, since it leads us straight to a perfect pattern of it. Barnes reads the connection the same way and adds that the hope will not merely incline a man toward holiness but be actually followed by that result.

On who does the purifying the voices divide by temperament. Barnes will not let the reflexive verb be read as independence — he does not deny that we depend on divine aid — but says the writer brings the agency of man into view as essentially connected with success, as the sacred writers often do. Robertson gives the word's history, that it was used of ceremonial purifications before the internal cleansing of heart and soul and self, and calls the process the work of both God and man. Clarke is more insistent: the apostle does not speak of any man purifying his own heart, because that is impossible, but of persevering in the purity into which the Lord has brought him — or else of anxiously using all the means that lead to it while imploring God for the sanctifying Spirit. Henry turns the verse into a test of the hope rather than of the effort, since the sons of God know their Lord is of purer eyes than to allow anything impure to dwell with him: it is the hope of hypocrites that makes allowance for gratifying impure desires.

The measure set by the last clause opens the sharpest disagreement in the chapter. Barnes argues the passage cannot teach sinless perfection in this life, because whatever it proves it proves of every one who has the hope, so the doctrine would not be that some Christians may become perfect but that all in fact do — which he presumes nobody will hold. What it does establish is that the tendency of the hope is to make a man pure, that all who cherish it will aim at the Saviour's own purity, and that the aim will at some future time be accomplished: the same kind of purity here, the same degree hereafter. Clarke takes the opposite side and takes it hotly. If the blood of Christ cleanses from all sin, and he was manifested to destroy the works of the devil, and sin is the work of the devil, then God means that believers shall be saved from all sin; and he asks those who deny it how much sin a man may be saved from, since the soul must have some determinate object in view and should not spend its faith praying for the unattainable. He charges the Westminster divines with laying every man under a fatal necessity of sinning in thought, word and deed, calls it a miserable salvo to say the regenerate sin less than they used to and only occasionally, and asks whether the grace that saved them partially could not save them perfectly. Robertson stands aside from the quarrel, noting only that the emphatic demonstrative refers to Christ, who can be called pure in virtue of the perfection of his humanity.
4:
Robertson notes that the article stands with both subject and predicate, making the terms coextensive and so interchangeable: sin is lawlessness and lawlessness is sin. Clarke widens the reach of that by the law's own summary — the spirit of the law as of the gospel is that we should love God with all our powers and our neighbour as ourselves, and since all disobedience is contrary to love, sin is transgression whether the act refers to God or to our neighbour. Wesley puts the aggravation in a clause, that by sinning a man sets God's authority at nought, which is implied in the very nature of sin. Henry defines it as a privation of agreement with the divine law — that law which is the transcript of the divine nature, contains God's will for the government of the world, and shows man the way of felicity and peace — so that the commission of sin is the rejection of the law, and thereby of the divine authority, and consequently of God himself.

Whether the sentence describes any single fault is a separate question, answered no. Gill grants the words are true of any sin great or small taken with what follows, but says what is designed here is a course of sinning, a wilful, obstinate persisting in it. Robertson reaches the same result from the participle, which is present and means the habit of doing sin, the converse of doing righteousness named just before. Barnes reconstructs the setting that made the point necessary, since the writer seems to be combating an opinion then current that men might sin and yet be true Christians; on what ground it was held he does not know, and lists the possibilities — that orthodoxy was all religion required, that nobody expected men to become holy in this life, that Christ came to relax the law and the freedom he procured was freedom to indulge, that Christians as heirs of all things had a right to enjoy all things, or that the passions are too strong to restrain. All of these, he observes, have been held under some form of Antinomianism, and the argument here would answer any of them.

Calvin supplies the excuse he thinks was actually being made: it is no wonder if we sin, because we are men, and there is a great difference between sin and iniquity. The definition dissipates that, since the word for sin may seem light while transgression of the law cannot appear so easily forgiven, the object being to produce hatred and horror of it. But Calvin is careful about what the definition does not do. It does not make all sins equal, and has nothing in common with the delirious paradoxes of the Stoics; nor does it mean offending in some instance, since the faithful, still tempted by the lusts of the flesh, are not free from sin and yet are not guilty of iniquity, because sin does not reign in them. To do or commit or practise sin is in this writer's language what being the servant of sin is in his Gospel — a prevailing and habitual course. What is hateful to God is the perverse life of those who indulge themselves in the liberty of sinning; the faithful are not to be called iniquitous, since they desire to obey, abhor their own vices, and form their life as far as in them lies according to the law. Barnes reaches the same standard from the other end, that the law measures our duty and so the degree of guilt when it is not obeyed, embracing what we omit where a thing is commanded as well as what we do where it is forbidden. Henry adds that the design of the argument is to fill the believer's mind with multiplied reasons against sin and against all communion with the unfruitful works of darkness.
5:
Gill takes the manifestation to be the incarnation itself: the Word who lay in the Father's bosom from all eternity was in the fulness of time made manifest in the flesh, assuming our nature into union with his divine person, and dwelt among men. Robertson confirms that the verb here refers to that appearing and not to the second coming, though it is the same form used a few lines earlier, and presses the verb for taking away: Isaiah uses a word for bearing sins, but this one means to lift up and carry off, and the noun is plural rather than collective. Barnes calls this the second argument of the paragraph and perhaps the strongest that can bear on a Christian's mind — that the Lord Jesus saw sin to be so great an evil that he gave himself to the bitter sorrows of the cross to redeem us from it. The whole work was designed to deliver us from the dominion of sin and not to furnish means of indulgence, so a man perverts the design of the coming who so interprets grace as to suppose it now lawful to indulge his passions. How, he asks, could we indulge in what crushed our Redeemer in death? Clarke sets out three things taken away — the power of sin destroyed, its guilt pardoned, its pollution cleansed — and asks whether Christ can be supposed unable or unwilling to accomplish the object of his own coming.

Calvin argues the taking away meant here is not remission. Elsewhere Christ takes away sins because he atoned for them so that they are not imputed; here he really and actually takes them away, since through him our old man is crucified and his Spirit by repentance mortifies the flesh — and the context requires that sense, since those who cease not to sin render void the benefits of Christ, who came to destroy the reigning power of sin. He adds that the writer speaks not of Christ personally but of his whole body, and that the renewal is not instantaneous but continues throughout life. Wesley wants the whole destroyed, root and branch, and reads the clause about Christ's own sinlessness to mean that he could not suffer on his own account but only to make us as himself. Gill fills out what abiding is: as the branch in the vine, deriving light and life and grace from Christ, dwelling in him by faith, rooted and grounded in him, taking up rest and security in him.

The denial that such a man sins is the difficulty, and Barnes brings three objections against reading it as sinless perfection. If it teaches that at all it teaches that every Christian is perfect, since the statement is of whosoever abides; that is not true, for who can maintain that Abraham or Moses or David or Paul never sinned after regeneration, and they never affirmed it of themselves; and the reading is not needed, since the language is such as any writer would use to say a man is not characteristically a sinner. Robertson supplies the grammar Barnes is reaching for: both verbs are linear presents, so the sense is does not keep on sinning, and the articular participle describes one who lives a life of sin rather than the occasional acts an aorist would name. Clarke gets the same result by another route, taking the tense in the last clause as a Hebrew preterite standing for a present — he who sins against God does not see him, the eye of his faith being darkened so that he no longer knows God as his portion. Calvin puts the positive side: faith in Christ is vainly pretended where there is no newness of life, for Christ is never dormant where he reigns, and puts sin to flight as the sun drives away darkness by its own brightness.
7:
Gill names the deceit guarded against as the Gnostic one, that knowledge without practice is enough and it is no matter how a man lives provided his notions are right. Robertson reads the imperative as continuous — let no one keep on leading you astray — and tells the readers to break the spell of any Gnostic charmer. Barnes takes the maxim that follows as great and undeniable, and presses it against every substitute: no matter how a man claims to be justified by faith, how he conforms to the rites of religion, how zealous he is for orthodoxy or for the order of the church, what raptures he has had or what peace he boasts of, how little he fears death, unless he is in fact righteous he cannot be a child of God. Barnes adds that such a man will always feel his claim is owed not to himself but to the grace of God. Calvin makes the same point as a test of profession: newness of life is testified by good works, and many persuade themselves they have righteousness buried in their hearts while iniquity occupies their feet and hands and tongue and eyes.

Clarke hears two deceits — either that you cannot be saved from sin in this life, or that sin cannot alter your state once you are adopted — and answers that a man is righteous according to his state and nature and the extent of his moral powers, allowing for the disparity between what is bounded and what is without limits. Wesley states the rule in a line, that none is righteous but he who uniformly practises righteousness. On the sentence that follows, Gill is careful that it not be read of any single act, since then every man would be of the devil, no man living without sin; what is meant is the man who makes sin his constant business, and who is of the devil not by generation but by imitation, resembling him as children do their parents. Barnes allows the words two senses: all who sin, believers included, resemble Satan so far as they are imperfect, since sin makes us resemble him wherever it exists — but the principal idea is that all who habitually sin belong to him.

The clause about the devil's beginning is guarded on two sides. Barnes denies it can mean he sinned from the beginning of his existence, since he was made holy like the other angels; he introduced sin into the universe and has practised it ever since. Robertson reaches the same by the tense, a linear progressive present meaning he has been sinning from the beginning of his career — this is his normal life, and those who imitate him become his spiritual children, though the conflict ends in certain victory over him. Calvin uses the verse to deny any middle condition, since Satan reigns wherever the righteousness of Christ has not the primacy; but he refuses the Manichean inference, since the devil is not wicked by nature but became so through defection, is not equal to God, and can do nothing except at the permission of his Creator. The beginning meant is not eternity, as when the Word is said to be from the beginning, but that the devil has been an apostate since the creation. Clarke turns the doctrine into a charge, that the devil maintains sin in the world by persuading men they cannot be saved from their sins in this life, so as to secure a residence in their hearts — knowing that if he has a place there through life he will probably have it at death, and if so through eternity. Calvin answers from the other side, since Pelagians and Catharians formerly made a wrong use of this passage and some Anabaptists have renewed the dotage, imagining the faithful endowed in this world with angelic purity.
9:
Augustine states the difficulty as a pastoral emergency. A man is pressed by two sayings out of the same letter: if he confesses himself a sinner he fears to hear that he is therefore not born of God; but if he says he has no sin he takes a blow from the other side, that we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. Placed in the midst, he cannot find what to say or confess. Augustine's first move is to close off one exit: to profess oneself without sin is not only full of peril but full of error — would that a man had none and could say so truly. Gill describes the birth rather than the difficulty — a being quickened and made partaker of the divine nature, owing not to the will of men but to grace, ascribed sometimes to the Father, sometimes to Christ who quickens whom he will, and chiefly to the Spirit, the author of the whole of sanctification. Wesley makes it a living faith by which God continually breathes spiritual life into the soul, and the soul breathes out love and prayer.

The seed that remains is the hinge, and its owner is disputed. Barnes gives both readings — that his may refer to the man, the principle being now properly his own, or to God, who implanted a germ of divine origin — and reports that Robinson, Macknight and Lucke take the second, which he thinks true. As to what the seed is, Augustine, Clemens and Grotius take it for the word of God; Barnes will not, since what abides in a Christian's heart is not the naked word but that word made vital by the Spirit. Two things follow: the germ abides as a constant vital principle, and it so continues that a man will not fall away and perish. Robertson agrees the seed is God's, quoting Vincent's phrase for it, the divine principle of life. Calvin takes the incorruptibility of that seed to be the answer to the hardest case, David's, who for a time laboured under such a stupor that not a spark of grace appeared: the seed may be stifled, but a live coal was hid under the ashes, and though Satan labours to root out whatever is of God in the elect, a hidden root remains.

On the flat impossibility of the last clause the voices divide. Robertson says the English is a mistranslation: the present infinitive can only mean he cannot go on sinning, not that he cannot commit a sin, for which the aorist would have been used — and adds that a great deal of false theology has grown out of a misunderstanding of the tense. Barnes reaches a similar sense without the grammar, taking cannot to mean a certainty as absolute as physical impossibility that the renewed will not be characteristically sinners. Clarke rejects that reading as bringing the privileges of the heavenly birth very low indeed, and tells the story of the physiognomist who examined Socrates and pronounced him the most gluttonous and brutal old man he had met — and, when the pupils turned on him, was defended by Socrates: the principles of his science may be correct, for such I was, but I have conquered it by my philosophy. Will Christian divines, Clarke asks, allow the grace of Christ a sway not so extensive as the philosophy of a heathen who never heard of the true God? Calvin turns the clause against the Sorbonists, who allow that the will cannot desire what is right unassisted but imagine a motion of the Spirit leaving us free choice, and so draw merits out of our willing obedience. This passage says otherwise: the Spirit's power is so effectual that it necessarily retains us in obedience, and continues to the last, so that inflexible perseverance is added to newness of life.
10:
Gill uses the verse to separate two things often run together: adoption is an act of God's sovereign will, secret in his own heart and antecedent to regeneration, so that regeneration and faith do not make men the children of God but manifest them to be so — adoption entitles them to the inheritance, regeneration gives them the nature of children, and that not to the world but to themselves and other saints. Barnes takes the sentence as a test of character with two parts, doing righteousness and loving the brethren, and suspects the singular pronoun intimates that an important part of righteousness consists in brotherly love. Robertson calls this the line of cleavage obvious to all, comparing the Pharisees who claimed Abraham while their conduct showed them children of the devil, and remarks that it is not a popular note with an age that wishes to remove all distinction between Christians and the world. Clarke calls it a fearful text and says we shall stand or fall by it whatever our creed may say; and on the second half he allows no narrow construction, since God made of one blood all the nations of men, so that all are of one family and consequently brethren.

Cyril reads the verse as a warning against a doctrine rather than a life. He will not tolerate those who give a wrong meaning to the saying about the children of God and of the devil, as if there were by nature some men to be saved and some to be lost; we come into that sonship not of necessity but by choice. Judas was not by nature a son of perdition, for he would never otherwise have cast out devils in Christ's name, since Satan does not cast out Satan; nor would Paul have turned from persecuting to preaching. The adoption is in our own power, he says, quoting the word that to as many as received him he gave power to become children of God — not before their believing but from it were they counted worthy to become such by their own choice. Calvin reads the manifestation in the other direction: those claim a place among the children of God in vain who do not prove themselves such by a holy life, though he does not mean they are so manifested as to be recognised by the whole world, only that the fruit of adoption always appears in the life. Since all whom God calls he regenerates by his Spirit, newness of life is a perpetual evidence of adoption. Wesley marks the turn, that here the writer passes from the general proposition to one particular.

Robertson notes that the word for message occurs in the New Testament only here and at the opening of the letter, and that the readers had this charge from the beginning of the gospel — it goes back to Cain and Abel, whom the next verse names. Barnes reports the variant between message and commandment and thinks it not material which is followed; the reference is to the law given by the Saviour as a permanent direction to his disciples. Henry commends the injunction from its antiquity, since it came among the principal parts of practical Christianity: we should love the Lord Jesus and value his love, and consequently love all the objects of it. Calvin explains why the whole of righteousness can be summed up in a single duty. The love of God holds the first place, but since love toward men depends on it the two are often put one for the other, a part for the whole; so every man endued with benevolence and humanity is thereby just, because love is the fulfilling of the law. He adds that the appeal to what they heard from the beginning shows the statement ought not to have seemed new to them.
12:
Gill explains why the example comes in here: brotherly love is illustrated by its contrary, and Cain was the first instance both of hating a brother and of fratricide, a very detestable one, by which the writer would dissuade men from so abominable a practice. Robertson makes the verb harsher than our version does — an old word for slaughtering, to cut the throat like an ox in the shambles, occurring elsewhere in the New Testament only in the Revelation — and notes that the interrogative is an unusual construction meaning for the sake of what. He also observes that the motive assigned is not in the narrative itself but an addition to it, though one that accords with what the letter to the Hebrews says of Abel's offering: jealousy led to murder. Wesley asks whether the brother was killed for any fault, and answers that it was just the reverse — he was killed for his goodness.

Calvin uses the example to correct a mistaken account of holiness. Men ever blunder as to the way of living, because they make holiness consist of fictitious works, and while they torment themselves with trifles they think themselves doubly acceptable to God — as the monks, who proudly call their mode of living a state of perfection. What the apostle testifies is that this righteousness alone is approved by God, that we love one another, and that the devil reigns where hatred, envy and enmity prevail; and since brotherly love proceeds from the love of God as an effect from a cause, it is commended here as the evidence of that love. Clarke turns the same principle on a larger crime. Who are they, he asks, who through pride, lust of power and gain murder each other in wars and political contentions? They too are of the wicked one, and to justify the principle or excuse the abettors of such wars is as vain as it is wicked; the message sent to man from the beginning was love one another and love your enemies, and surely that does not mean blow out their brains. Barnes reaches the same conclusion more quietly, that a large part of the crimes of the earth have been caused, as in this murder, by want of brotherly love, and nothing but love would be needed to end them.

The hatred of the world is treated as ordinary rather than surprising. Robertson notes that the imperative is present and negative, so the sense is not do not begin to wonder but cease wondering, and that the same language stands in the Lord's own words to the disciples. Barnes puts the emphasis on the pronoun: as Cain hated his brother without cause, so they were not to think it strange that the world hated them likewise. He observes that the Saviour introduced these two subjects in the same connexion, enjoining brotherly love and telling them in the same breath that the world hated him before it hated them — the object being to show the necessity of strong mutual affection among Christians, since they can hope for none from the world. Gill gives the history of it: the enmity began upon the fall, between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent, showed itself in Cain, appeared when Ishmael persecuted Isaac, and continued when the Jews persecuted the prophets and hated Christ, so that this is the common lot of all who will live godly and should not be reckoned strange. Clarke reads the verse as a lesson to the church preparatory to martyrdom, since neither justice nor mercy is to be expected from enemies of God — they are either full of malice and envy or else specious, hollow and deceitful — and closes with a line of verse, that a foe to God was ne'er true friend to man.
14:
Gill sets out the death left behind. There is a moral death, lying in separation from God, in loss of the image of righteousness in which man was created, and in a servitude to sin which is itself death; and a legal death, the sentence under which all stand as considered in Adam. Regeneration is a resurrection, by which they pass to a life of sanctification, of justification, and of communion with Christ. Clarke reads the verb as a change of residence, death and life being two kingdoms whose inhabitants may be removed from one to the other, and compares Paul's word about translation into the kingdom of the Son of his love; those addressed had once lived in the region and shadow of death and had crossed into a kingdom where life and love prevail. Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun, the Christian consciousness set against the unregenerate world, and the perfect tense — the passage has already been made, here on earth. Cyril quotes the phrase for its speed: the righteous were many years in pleasing God, but what they gained by long well-pleasing Christ bestows in a single hour, and he who saved the robber on Golgotha after one hour of belief will save any believer.

That love is evidence and not cause is insisted on carefully. Calvin says the argument is drawn from the sign and not the cause, since no one sincerely loves the brethren except he is regenerated by the Spirit, so love is a sure symbol of regeneration; but it would be preposterous to infer that life is obtained by love, which is in order of time posterior to it. He allows the milder claim, that love makes us more certain of life, and answers it too: though faith is confirmed by all the graces of God as aids, its foundation is his mercy only — as when we enjoy the light we are certain the sun shines, and see it more clearly when its rays fall where we stand, yet even when no ray reaches us we are satisfied that it shines for our benefit. Robertson makes the distinction grammatically, that the conjunction gives the proof of the transition and not its ground. Barnes calls the test infallible and wonders it is not more used, since a man can judge whether he loves a Christian because he bears the image of the Saviour, and whether he can look beyond the bounds of his own sect and be pleased with the Christian character wherever it is found. Wesley states it the other way: we could not love our brethren unless we were passed from death to life.

Henry is chiefly concerned to say what this love is not. It is not a zeal for a party, nor an affection for — still less an affectation of — those who share our denomination. It supposes a general love to mankind, the law of Christian love being founded on the catholic law of loving one's neighbour as oneself; and mankind is to be loved on two accounts, as the excellent work of God made in resemblance of him, which is the reason assigned for punishing a murderer, and as beloved in some measure in Christ, the whole race having a Redeemer designed for it. A world so beloved of God should be loved by us, and that love will exert itself in prayers for the conversion of the yet uncalled world, and will include due love to enemies. Only then does it include a peculiar love to the Christian society, and that for her head's sake, believers being loved not so much for themselves as for the sake of God and Christ, who have loved them. Barnes and Clarke agree what the failure proves: the man who does not love remains dead in sins, or as Clarke puts it, has never changed his original residence.
15:
Gill calls the hater a soul murderer, and locates the crime where the Sermon on the Mount locates adultery — he murders his brother in his heart, since not only taking life but causeless anger and malice breaks the sixth commandment. Barnes reads it as a statement about tendency rather than equivalence: the writer does not say a man who hates without killing is guilty to the same degree, but that the spirit which would lead to murder is present, and nothing is wanting but the removal of outward restraint. It is a fearful declaration, since there are then many real murderers on earth besides those detected — and who has not at some period indulged hatred and envy which, acted out, would have led to taking life? Calvin insists the charge is not hyperbolical, since we wish him to perish whom we hate; it does not matter that a man keeps his hands from mischief, for even wishing evil to befall a brother from someone else makes us murderers. Robertson notes that the compound noun goes back to Euripides and occurs in the New Testament only here and of Satan.

Clarke enters a caution against a use made of the next clause. It has been quoted to prove that no murderer can be saved, which the text does not say; there have been many instances of men guilty of murder who found genuine repentance and mercy from him who prayed Father, forgive them. It is nevertheless an awful text, he says, for those who shed blood on frivolous pretences, or in wars which have their origin in the worst passions of the human heart. Wesley allows no middle ground — there is no medium between loving and hating a brother, and every degree of hatred is a degree of the same temper that moved Cain. On the verse that follows, several notice that the words of God are not in the Greek. Gill reports the versions that carry it and those reading simply his love to us; Barnes thinks the addition should never have entered the translation, since it would convey the idea that the divine nature suffered, and the original is more expressive without it — by this we know love, seen in its highest form when the Son of God gave himself to die.

Wesley makes the omission eloquent, comparing Mary at the tomb saying to the gardener, Sir, if thou hast borne him hence: there is an emphatical language even in silence, declaring how totally the thoughts were possessed by the subject. Calvin takes the death of Christ as the standard, and is careful how far the comparison runs. Our love is approved when we transfer the love of ourselves to our brethren, so that every one, in a manner forgetting himself, seeks the good of others; but we are far from equal to Christ, and to require it would drive us to despair, so what is asked is that we follow his steps at a distance. Nor is the benefit of our death the same, for God's wrath is not pacified by our blood — the comparison concerns not the effect of his death but the forming of our life on his example. Robertson agrees that our laying down our lives has no atoning value as his had, but is a supreme proof of love. Barnes gives a principle for when the duty applies, that we should do it where a greater good results from the sacrifice than from guarding our own lives, as a physician stays with a pestilence; and he recalls what the world said of the early Christians, behold how they love one another and are ready to die for one another. Henry names the thing plainly as the condescension, the miracle and the mystery of divine love, that God would redeem the church with his own blood.
17:
Gill takes the world's good to mean any share of the outward enjoyments of life, noting that one version renders the phrase as though it pointed at a man in high office who is both great and rich, though the words are not to be restricted so; of a man who has nothing to spare it is not required. Robertson confirms the sense from the noun, which means livelihood rather than the principle of life, and finds the picture sharpened by the tense — an aorist replacing the present, the graphic slamming of the door of his compassion. The word rendered bowels means the nobler viscera, and the closing question is rhetorical: it is the practical, not the speculative, that counts in the hour of need. Barnes explains why the seat of mercy is named, since that part is affected when the mind feels compassion, and states the argument plainly — if we ought to be willing to lay down our lives, we ought to make the far smaller sacrifices that relieve distress. Clarke puts it as a test: if we do not divide our bread with the hungry we would certainly not lay down our life for him, and hardheartedness and the love of God never meet.

Calvin draws four propositions out of the verse. No one truly loves his brethren except he shows it whenever occasion occurs; every man is bound to assist so far as he has means; the necessity of each is to be seen to, since a man requires our aid precisely as he needs the food of which we have abundance; and no act of kindness is pleasing to God unless accompanied with sympathy. That last is the one he presses, since many apparently liberal men do not feel for the miseries of their brethren, whereas what is required is that we sympathise with others in their evils no otherwise than as though they were our own. He also explains why the love of God is named where brotherly love is in question: love to God cannot but generate love of the brethren, and God tries our love to him by bidding us love men out of regard to himself. Wesley adds two strokes of his own — that the very sight of want knocks at the door of the spectator's heart, and that the man here described shuts it up whether he is asked or not.

On loving in deed rather than word they are unanimous in substance and careful in the same way. Calvin says there is a concession in the first clause, since we cannot really love in tongue only, and that the word only is understood there, as often in Scripture; he notes the correspondence of the members, word answering to truth and tongue to work, and quotes with approval the remark that the apostle cannot be supposed to forbid affectionate speeches to brethren in distress, but forbids us to content ourselves with them. Robertson makes the same qualification, that kind words which comfort and cheer are not condemned, but warm words should be accompanied by warm deeds — a case where actions speak louder than words. Gill says it is lawful and right to express love in words, especially to persons in distress, but that this must not be all, since it is of no avail to tell such a man to be warmed and filled while giving him nothing to warm and fill him with. Clarke quotes a rabbinical saying to the same effect: if love consisted in word only, then love would cease as soon as the word was pronounced, and such was the love between Balak and Balaam; but if love consists not in word it cannot be dissolved, and such was the love of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and the patriarchs before them.
19:
Augustine takes up the question the previous verse leaves open: in what work, or in what truth, is the man known who loves God or his brother? He has already said where charity is perfected, in the laying down of a life for friends, and grants that nothing greater can be found. But since it is not perfect in all, he will not let a man despair in whom it is imperfect, provided that be already born which may be perfected — for once born it must be nourished, and by feeding of its own kind brought to maturity. So he asks instead where charity begins, and answers from the verse about the man who has this world's goods and closes his heart. Gill reads the evidence as a cause known by its effect: loving one another in deed, the saints learn that they belong to God, who is truth itself, to Christ who is the truth, and to the gospel, which is the word of truth. Wesley calls it a further proof by real, operative kindness, and adds a lexical observation worth keeping — that heart in this writer's vocabulary means conscience, a term never appearing in his writings.

Barnes explains the verb rendered assure, which properly means persuade, and is used of bringing over one who has unkind or prejudiced feelings, and so of conciliating and quieting. The sense here is that by furnishing evidence of genuine piety we allay the agitations of the mind and soothe an accusing conscience. He does not pretend the accusation is baseless: a true believer never denies that much in his past might justly indict him, yet finds despite it that he is God's child, and rests satisfied that all will end well. Clarke makes the test turn on what a man can and cannot fake. Nobody can impose upon himself by imagining an affection he lacks; he may make empty professions to others, but whoever loves God or man knows it because he feels it, and an unfelt affection is mere word or tongue. This, Clarke says, is the strongest and most infallible test of a man's Christianity. Robertson notes that the verb for knowing is future — at any future emergency we shall come to know by this — and that the assurance is had in the very presence of God, because God understands us.

Calvin accepts none of that as a foundation, though he welcomes it as a support. Charity does not yield the knowledge the apostle speaks of, as though from it we might extract the certainty of salvation; we learn our sonship no otherwise than as God seals his free adoption on the heart by his own Spirit, and as faith receives the sure pledge offered in Christ. Charity is accessory, an inferior aid, a prop and not a foundation. Why then is the evidence appealed to at all? Because faith cannot exist without a clear conscience — not that certainty springs from one, but that union with God is really and not falsely felt only where the Spirit manifests himself in our charity; the apostle is condemning feigned profession, and denies that any genuine persuasion is possible where the Spirit yields no such fruit. Yet nobody should conclude that we must look to works in order to be sure. Augustine holds the two together by making charity a thing born small and grown; Barnes, by saying the evidence quiets the accusation rather than answers it.
20:
Henry reads the verse as establishing a court and asserting its authority. The heart here is our self-reflecting judicial power, by which we take cognizance of our own dispositions and actions and pass sentence on our state toward God; it acts as witness, judge and executioner, accusing or excusing, and holds that office by divine appointment, the spirit of man being the candle of the Lord which searches the inward parts. Conscience is God's vicegerent, calling the court in his name, and God is chief Judge in it, so that the act of the court is his act. Gill puts the same threefold office briefly: the inward witness accuses of the evil of sin, is as good as a thousand witnesses, and on its own testimony pronounces guilty. Robertson observes that the verb for condemning occurs only three times in the New Testament, and that the omniscience appealed to here is linked with divine love and sympathy rather than set against it; he quotes Brooke's remark that this difficult passage strikes the very centre of Christian truth.

What follows is a sentence from a higher bench. Clarke says God knows every hypocritical winding and turning of the soul, tries the reins, and sees the deceitfulness we cannot see and could not comprehend if we could; being the just Judge he will condemn us more strictly than we can condemn ourselves. Wesley calls him an infinitely holier and more impartial Judge, so that there is no hope of hiding anything. Calvin takes the comparison to be one of judgment specifically, God searching more minutely, and cites Paul's word that though he knew nothing against himself he was not thereby justified — for however attentive to his office he erred in many things and was through inadvertence ignorant of faults God perceived. The meaning, on Calvin's reading, is simply that since divine knowledge penetrates deeper than our own perception, no man can stand before him unless the integrity of his heart sustains him. Barnes presses the corollary: we cannot purchase quiet by supposing God fails to see what troubles us, since he knows the sins we have forgotten and those we persuade ourselves are not sinful, and looks on all with less allowance than we do.

Two opposite readers need answering, and between them the commentators answer both. To the trembling soul who fears that a self-accusing heart guarantees divine condemnation, Henry replies that the errors of the witness are not reckoned as acts of the court: ignorance, prejudice and presumption are faults of the officers or of a jury returning a false verdict, not of the judge, since self-consciousness properly so called does not include acts of mistaken power. What is bound in a rightly constituted court is bound in heaven — so let the inward witness be well informed, be heard, and be diligently attended to. To the presumptuous, Calvin observes that the reprobate are sometimes sunk by Satan into such stupor that they no longer perceive their own evils and rush without alarm into perdition, and that hypocrites, inebriated by a false conceit of their righteousness, feel no convictions at all. The answer is not difficult: hypocrites are deceived because they shun the light, the reprobate feel nothing because they have departed from God, and there is no security for a bad conscience except in hiding-places — whereas the apostle speaks of men whom God draws forth to the light and forces to his tribunal. Barnes adds the distinction that keeps the verse usable, that the reference is less to our past lives than to our present deportment: in view of past guilt peace may be found by evidences of piety, but no external act will soothe a heart that condemns us for secret sin indulged now.
21:
Gill is careful to say what an unaccusing heart is not. It is not the stupidity of mind found in men who have no sense of sin, nor the state of those past feeling whose consciences are seared; nor does it mean such purity of life that a believer's heart never reproaches him, since that perfection is not attainable here. What is meant is a conscience purged by the blood of Christ, which speaks peace and pardon. Robertson agrees the clause is the converse of the one before it but no claim to sinlessness — it describes the consciousness of fellowship in God's presence, and the boldness it yields extends even to prayer. Barnes explains the noun as properly openness in speaking one's sentiments, and enters the same guard: the writer does not mean we have confidence toward God on the ground of what we do, as if it constituted a claim on his favour, but that we may so live as to have evidence of piety and hope of acceptance. Clarke sums it up — if we are conscious of our own sincerity, practising no deceit and using no mask, we can appeal to God and come boldly to the throne of grace.

Calvin raises the objection this invites: who can be found whose heart reproves him in nothing? His answer is that the godly are reproved in such a way that they may at the same time be absolved: they must be seriously troubled inwardly for their sins, so that terror may lead them to humility and self-hatred, but they presently flee to the sacrifice of Christ, where they have sure peace. In another sense they are not condemned, since however deficient they confess themselves, they are relieved by the testimony that they truly fear God and desire to submit to his righteousness; all who possess that feeling may justly be said to have a peaceful heart. Calvin also distinguishes this from Paul, who shows the cause of confidence where this writer names only an inseparable addition. Wesley describes the same faculty as duly enlightened by the word and Spirit of God, comparing our thoughts and words and works with that word and pronouncing that they agree. Henry adds that such men come as children to a reconciled Father and may ask what they will.

The promise that follows is read by all with limits. Barnes states two, that we ask in a proper manner and that the thing asked be such as God sees consistent to give, and adds that obedience is not the ground of being heard but the evidence that we are his children — a parent being disposed to favour dutiful children. Robertson finds no limitation in the form of the words save complete fellowship with God, which means complete surrender of our will to his, and remarks that the answer may not come in the shape we expect but will be better. Clarke identifies the commandments as loving God and loving our neighbour, the great commandments of both covenants, since whoever is filled with that love will do what pleases God — love being the very soul of obedience; he notes too that heart in these verses stands for conscience, and that the Greek fathers so interpret it, Origen and Oecumenius among them. Calvin uses the verse to shut the door against hypocrites, that they may not rush into God's presence in contempt of him, but repeats his guard against reading the condition as a ground: woe to us if we look on works, which have nothing in them but cause for fear, since the faithful can come to God's tribunal only by relying on Christ the Mediator. The causal particle marks an inseparable companion rather than a cause, as when one says that because the sun shines at midday there is more heat — though heat comes not from light.
23:
Two things are named and yet the noun is singular, and that is deliberate. Gill says the two are reduced to one because inseparable — where one is, the other is, since faith works by love. Calvin notes the singular for the same reason, that the writer does not separate faith from love but requires both, and calls the verse remarkable for defining briefly wherein the whole perfection of a holy life consists: God does not lead us through labyrinths but sets before us shortly what he approves, and in that brevity there is no obscurity. Barnes calls it his commandment by way of eminence, the injunction lying at the foundation of all obedience. Wesley calls it all the commandments in one word, the greatest that ever issued from the throne of glory — if neglected no other can be kept, if observed all others are easy. Robertson notes that the manuscripts divide between aorist and present for the verb of believing, a crisis or the continuous tenor of a life, and that the name stands for all that Christ is, what Westcott called a compressed creed.

Henry breaks the believing into four acts: to discern what Christ is according to his name; to approve him in judgment as one wonderfully adapted to the whole work of salvation; to consent to him and acquiesce in him as our recoverer unto God; and to rely on him for the full discharge of that saving office. He explains why this is required of one who would prevail in prayer, since it is by the Son that we come to the Father — through his purchase our blessings come, through his intercession our prayers are heard. Calvin fastens on the word name, which he takes of preaching: few understand what it is to believe on Christ, but the only right faith embraces him as he is set forth in the gospel, so there is no faith without teaching. Clarke states its content, that for the sake of his death we are justified from all things from which the law could not justify us — and adds that without a renewal of the heart love to God and man is impossible, and that renewal comes by Christ. Cyril dwells on the dignity of the title conferred: since God himself is called Faithful, as he is called Good and Almighty, a man receiving that name becomes partaker of a title of God.

On the indwelling, Robertson quotes Bede — let God be a home to thee, and be thou the home of God — and observes that this is the first mention of the Spirit in the letter, regretting that our English keeps the grammatical gender, reading which for whom. How the indwelling is known divides them sharply. Barnes takes it to be known only by effects: the Spirit enlightens the mind, elevates the affections, sustains in trial and quickens in duty, and where those exist we may be certain he is present, since none can determine that he dwells in them except by what is produced in the life. Clarke will not stop there. It was not by conjecture that Christians of old knew they stood in God's favour but by the testimony of his own Spirit, which is not only manifest by its effects but bears its own witness to its own indwelling, so a man knows he has it by direct witness as well as by fruits; how that testimony is given is inexplicable, as the wind blows where it lists, but every good man feels it. Calvin sets the verse beside Paul's: Paul speaks of the certainty of gratuitous adoption sealed on our hearts, while this writer regards the effects the Spirit produces while dwelling in us — and whatever good works we do proceed from his grace, the Spirit being not obtained by our righteousness but freely given.
